The War in Ethiopia
1
Al Jazeera

Fighting widens across Ethiopia as Tigray clashes escalate into war

Fighting spread across Ethiopia's Tigray, Afar and Amhara regions after a new seven-group rebel coalition, the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, launched coordinated operations against federal forces, seizing airports and capturing the Abala district in Afar. The alliance groups the Tigray People's Liberation Front with the Amhara Fano National Movement, the Oromo Liberation Army and fighters from the Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz regions, threatening the November 2022 peace deal. TPLF spokesman Abdisalam Balema said federal forces had “begun an offensive around southern Tigray… We will assess it,” and a day later called it a “full war.”

The Washington Post

Fears of renewed civil war grow in Ethiopia as fighting reignites

Renewed fighting between Ethiopia's federal government and Tigrayan forces stoked fears of a return to the 2020-2022 civil war that killed more than half a million people, The Washington Post reported. Tigrayan rebels said they were responding to a “full-scale offensive” by the government, while Addis Ababa countered that it was the rebels who started the fighting. The clashes, which erupted around September 23, mark the most serious rupture yet of the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement.

Al Jazeera (Opinion)

Ethiopia's new rebel alliance faces an old problem

In an opinion piece for Al Jazeera, Horn of Africa researcher Mohamed Kheir Omer argued that Ethiopia's newly formed seven-group rebel coalition, the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival — uniting the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement, the Oromo Liberation Army and forces from the Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz regions — risks repeating the fate of a similar coalition that fractured in 2021 over territorial disputes. Omer wrote that Ethiopia's recurring crises stem from a pattern in which “those who feel disadvantaged take up arms to change the status quo,” concluding that “removing Abiy would settle none of the arguments over land, command and constitutional power.”

One assessment described Eritrea's shift “from pariah state in the Horn to king-maker.”

Gebru, 27, said he was detained by recruiters before his parents paid to free him: “My parents found a way to get me released by paying 20,000 [Ethiopian] birr ($123) in cash.” Human Rights Watch's Laetitia Bader said the group had documented cases where “both former fighters but also civilians – young men, sometimes boys – were being abducted, detained,” including recruitment of minors as young as 15.

Is the Horn of Africa about to explode?

In an episode published September 25, The Fourcast examined resurgent tensions in the Horn of Africa following the 2020-2022 war between Tigrayan forces and the Ethiopian government that killed hundreds of thousands. Hosts Krishnan Guru-Murthy and Matt Frei, joined by Ethiopian journalist and Addis Standard founder Tsedale Lemma and former Royal African Society director Nicholas Westcott, discussed the formation of the seven-group “Alliance for Survival,” the seizure of three Tigray airports that prompted Ethiopian Airlines to suspend regional flights, and Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's strategic push for Red Sea access.

The BBC explained why Britain was reviewing its Chagos Islands sovereignty deal with Mauritius after US President Donald Trump called the agreement “terrible” during talks with UK leader Andy Burnham. The 2025 deal would have Britain pay Mauritius roughly £120 million a year over a 99-year lease to retain the Diego Garcia military base, with payments now suspended pending review. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said Trump's objections “provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing.”

Twelve of the 13 bodies were burned beyond recognition.

Democratic Republic of the Congo Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka told the UN General Assembly that despite diplomatic progress, real peace has not reached her country's people, saying “for millions of Congolese, this peace remains only a promise.” She accused Rwanda of waging “a war of aggression” through the M23 armed group and said the June 2025 DRC-Rwanda peace agreement's commitments remain unfulfilled, calling for implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 2773, which mandates a halt to hostilities and withdrawal of Rwandan forces.

48The Guardian

New records force Britain to confront its slave-trade past

The Guardian reported on newly compiled historical records — a 636-page register of British slave traders and nearly 4 million searchable records of enslaved people across 20 former British colonies — that revealed how deeply Britain's financial and civic institutions were entangled in the slave trade. Guardian community affairs correspondent Chris Osuh wrote that the documents show “a lot of amnesia about inconvenient histories” obscuring Britain's reliance on unpaid labour, noting the Royal African Company trafficked more Africans than any other trading firm.

49The Guardian

Africa 'hasn't decolonised education enough,' says health expert Nkengasong

Dr John Nkengasong, the Cameroonian virologist who formerly led Africa CDC and now serves as education director at the Mastercard Foundation, told the Guardian that “Africa hasn't decolonised its educational system enough” to harness the potential of the continent's youth, 70% of whom are under 30. He said sub-Saharan African countries spend 3.6 times more on debt than on education and that only 16% of African tertiary graduates transitioned smoothly into work in one study, arguing “no modern or ancient country has developed without a strong higher education system.”
